purpose: Voriconazole is used to treat serious fungal infections, especially in people whose immune systems are weakened, such as those going through chemotherapy or organ transplants. It is commonly used to treat infections caused by Aspergillus and Candida fungi. Your doctor may also use it to prevent fungal infections in high-risk patients.
how_it_works: Voriconazole works by blocking a key step that fungi need to build their outer protective layer called the cell membrane. Without this protective layer, the fungal cell falls apart and dies. Think of it like removing the walls of a house — without them, the structure cannot survive.
common_side_effects: Visual changes such as blurred vision or seeing colors differently (very common but usually temporary), sensitivity to light, skin rash, nausea, vomiting, headache, and elevated liver enzymes. Some people also notice a flushing or warm feeling in the skin when exposed to sunlight.
warnings: This medication can cause serious liver problems, so your doctor will check your liver with blood tests regularly. It can also make your skin very sensitive to the sun, so wear sunscreen and protective clothing outdoors. Voriconazole interacts with MANY other medications, so always tell your doctor and pharmacist everything you are taking. It should not be used during pregnancy as it can harm an unborn baby. It may also affect your heart rhythm, so tell your doctor if you have heart problems.
typical_dosing: The dose depends on your weight, the type of infection, and whether you are taking it by mouth or through an IV. A typical adult oral dose is 200 mg twice daily, taken at least one hour before or after a meal. Your doctor will determine the exact dose and duration that is right for you, so always follow their instructions carefully.
